Composed by the Śramaṇa Ke guan of Yunjian;
verified by the Dharma-grandson Zhi zeng of Shanyin.
The Ten Chapters on the Meaning of the *Jinfu* (Golden Scalpel) on the "Dual Wandering":
General and Specific Explanations by Master Yue.
This chapter was recorded as it was spoken during the course of a lecture, with notes taken by those listening.
The "Dual Wandering" (Śaṅgama) originally derives from the "Parable of the Birds" chapter (*Śakuntaka-parivarta*) of the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*.

This commentary explains the various difficult passages to demonstrate the universal application of the principle of "perfect identity. Among those who have lectured on this in the past, few have spoken of it;

it has been transmitted that only the former masters of Yongjia frequently expounded upon it, yet there were but few written expositions (*yi-zhang*). I have long applied my mind to this text, and now I shall briefly examine and discuss it, dividing it as follows:

Second, first distinguishing the two schools according to their respective positions, and then clarifying the original intent of their dual functions. This first section is further divided into two parts:
first, recounting what each school asserts; second, evaluating the perspectives of the two schools.
In the initial exposition, it first states that regarding Zhi-jue’s *Commentary on the Profound Meaning* (*Miaozong*) within the context of the "Ten Admonitions," it says:

"The judgment of our school concerning the 'sixteen-foot' and the 'venerable special' (zuntè) bodies does not divide them based on the quantity of their physical characteristics; rather, they are distinguished by the response and stimulus between the ultimate truth (*zhēn*) and the conventional (*zhōng*).

Since the Fourth Master [Zhi-yi] has already made this distinction, there is no need for the birth-body (*shēngshēn*) venerable special body to actually manifest in a massive form; it is sufficient to rely upon the sixteen-foot form."

Regarding the manifestation of the six types of birth-bodies and the *zhunti* (exalted special body) as commonly explained: Jingjue’s admonition states that there must be provisional and ultimate aspects, with distinctions of superiority and inferiority;
yet they should coexist. The birth-body is properly employed as a skillful means, while the *zhunti* is properly employed as the true reward.

Those of the Perfect Teaching understand that it is but a single dharma-substance that gives rise to two modes of application. Since the application is identical to the substance, the single characteristic cannot be apprehended within the substance itself.
Because they are employed in practice, the various marks appear vividly; even the Great Master spoke of the "marks of the dung beetle" (kīṭa-kṛmi).

Ultimately, for what reason must the "marks of the birth-body" (janma-kāya) necessarily be the "marks of the honored and special body" (vairocana-kāya)? Regarding the two birds of the constant and the inconstant flying together as one pair, how are they to be distinguished?
The Pure Awakening [Commentary] states that the inconstant birth-body in the Shared Residence (sahā-loka) corresponds to the Expedient Means (upāya).

The true recompense body (*sambhogakāya*) and the constant body of supreme excellence (*vairocana-vigraha*) can only be distinguished as two distinct functions when they are contrasted in this manner;
if the birth-body (*janmakāya*) were identical to the body of supreme excellence, then these two functions could not be distinguished. This is what Jingjue taught.

Furthermore, in his *Commentary on the Refutation of Slander*, Siming cites the interpretation from the *Original Commentary* (Ben-shu), stating: "Within the phenomena and principle, and the middle and extremes, they are neither two nor non-two."

Within these three cycles, the two functions are fully encompassed; whether it be body, land, person, or dharma, each one is complete with both functions, which mutually pervade and mutually include one another.
It continues until it says: "The student should know that by attaining only impermanence, one loses the function of permanence;
by attaining the function of permanence, the two functions are doubly fused. If one does not clarify this according to the timely teachings, [one will fail].
If one merely follows the manifest physical forms to make distinctions, then the meaning of the two functions—perfect and subtle—will forever remain submerged.

Zhiyi [Siming] intended this to demonstrate that all phenomena universally possess the meaning of these two functions; thus, the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is itself the honored, sublime body (*vairocana-kāya*).
This is what Siming taught. Next, regarding the evaluation: it is simply that in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the two birds fly together, representing the eternal and the non-eternal.
Although the two applications established by the two schools are as contradictory as arrows and stones, there is none that is not cited and employed;

this is truly because the perspectives of the two schools differ. Jingjue merely takes up the aspect of "discrimination" (fenbie) to explain it, completely losing the point that the two applications are mutually identical.
Now I ask: regarding the two applications in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which are illustrated by the metaphor of the two birds flying together, does this refer to "discrimination"?
To grasp at characteristics is precisely what constitutes the two functions; yet, by grasping at them while treating them as identical, one instead falls back into conceptual discrimination.

Thus, one knows that the loss of pure awakening is even more severe. To speak broadly, although conceptual discrimination may be permissible if its characteristics are seen as identical, this directly contradicts what one has established for oneself.
To speak decisively, even conceptual discrimination is a loss. Why? Because although one discriminates between the two functions, those two functions ought to be [identical].

Regarding the identity of the two bodies, their characteristics are not the same; whereas the provisional teachings of the Four Clarities (Sì míng) hold that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is identical to the honored body with marks (*lakṣaṇa-kāya*), this correctly captures the intended meaning of the two functions.

As for the primary metaphor of their mutual interpenetration, those who require further discussion—such as the claim by the Four Clarities that the birth-body is identical to the honored body—are asserting that the impermanent is identical to the permanent.
If the permanent were identical to the impermanent, then one could likewise say that the honored body is identical to the birth-body.

If it were otherwise, one might say that these teachings need not even be heard; how much less could the bodies manifested in the stages of Expedient Means (*upāya*) and True Reward (*vipākaphala*) be identical to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) of the Shared Residence?

If you say they cannot be considered identical, why then do you maintain this teaching that the birth-body is identical to the Honored Special Body (*viśeṣa-kāya*), that the impermanent is identical to the permanent, that the permanent is naturally identical to the impermanent, and that the birth-body is identical to the Honored Special Body?
Furthermore, regarding the two types of *zhuntè* (extraordinary manifestations) within the four teachings concerning the birth-body (*shēngshēn*):

while it can be said that the manifested *zhuntè* is "the impermanent is itself the permanent," how can one say that the manifested *zhuntè* is "identical" (*xiāngjí*) [to the birth-body]? This seems difficult to comprehend;
I do not yet understand how the explanations of the four teachings can harmoniously accommodate the meaning of mutual identity. This point shall await further discussion below.
Clarification.

Next, the original intent of the two functions is clarified, which is further divided into two parts: first, presenting the textual passages on the two functions; second, clarifying the meaning of the two functions.
Regarding the presentation of the texts, one first presents the scriptural commentaries and subsequently determines the metaphors; the scriptural text is exactly as explained in the *Shiqian*.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, in the "Parable of the Birds" chapter, states: "Good son, there are two kinds of birds:
the first is named the *kalaviṅka* and the second is named the ruddy sheldrake (*cakravāka*). They dwell and move together, never parting from one another.

The reason this parable is set forth in the sūtra is to answer the question previously asked by Kāśyapa: "How does one practice together with the noble ones? Furthermore, as the sūtra says: "In accordance with the existence of sentient beings..."
In places where beings are to be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests birth therein; yet though he manifests birth, in reality there is no birth.
For this reason, the Tathāgata clearly abides in the eternal Dharma, like the *kalaviṅka* or the ruddy sheldrake. This is the brief citation from the sutra text.
As for the subsequent commentary (*śū*), it is exactly as cited in the *Shiqian* (The Commentary on the Profound Meaning). What is here called "wandering in pairs" refers to saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Within the bowl, both the permanent and the impermanent are present; the lower and the higher, moving together and resting side by side, signify that phenomena and principle are mutually identical, and duality is identical with the Middle, while the Middle is identical with duality.
Thus, within non-duality, duality is realized, and the meanings of phenomena and principle, as well as female and male, are simultaneously established.
According to the original commentary, it should state: "Birth-and-death is both permanent and impermanent, and Nirvana is likewise; the lower and the higher move together."
The cessation of phenomena is itself principle, and principle is itself phenomena; the two truths are themselves the Middle, and the Middle is itself the two truths.
It is not that there are two middles, yet the two middles are present. Thus, the meaning of "traversing both" is established, and the "male and female" (the dual) is also established.

Once the meaning of traversing both phenomena and principle is established, then from the stage of names and conceptual practice up to the ultimate realization, traversing both is fully accomplished. There is nothing lacking in this completeness of both the horizontal and the vertical.
Having omitted the above, I shall briefly extract from the commentary the definitive dharma and its analogy. In the Sūtra, the "simile" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the matter of the two birds flying together;

the "dharma illustrated" (*dārṣṭāntika*) is the shared noble practice (*sādhāraṇāryacaryā*). If this simile illustrates the shared noble practice, it refers to that which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas;
this is somewhat restricted. Regarding what is restricted in their cultivation, as stated in the *Sishiming* (The Four Clarities), whether it be the body or the land...
If a person is such that each and every dharma is fully complete, and the two functions mutually pervade and mutually encompass one another,

then this is profoundly penetrating and permeates all dharmas. One should know that although the scriptural text is restricted to using a metaphor for the shared noble practice (*sādhāraṇa-āryacaryā*),
the meaning of "traversing both" is further pervasive, universally encompassing everything because its essence— which is neither permanent nor impermanent— pervasively encompasses all.
Therefore, all dharmas can be both permanent and impermanent.

Next, the meaning of the two functions is clarified, which is further divided into two parts: first, a critique of the old [interpretations], and second, the elucidation of the present [position]. Regarding the critique of the old:
according to the treatises of former scholars, there were two meanings—first, the mutual opposition of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, and second, the simultaneous engagement with both.

Regarding the first meaning of "simultaneous cessation" (*pingxi*) as "relative": because *nirvāṇa* is the phenomenon (*shi*) that is itself the principle (*li*), and *saṃsāra* is the principle that is itself the phenomenon;

within the principle of *nirvāṇa*, both functions are fully present. This is based on the relativity of phenomenon and principle; the same applies to the subsequent two meanings of "middle and extremes" (*zhongbian*) and "extinction and illumination" (*wangzhao*).
Next, regarding "simultaneous cessation" as "mutual roaming" (*shuangyou*): this takes mutual roaming as the phenomenon, corresponding to the above.
The cessation of both extremes and the simultaneous stilling of the two middles—this is the function of these two returning to the essence.

Regarding the principle that "the two are the middle and yet not the middle," those of former times who made this statement committed two errors: first, they confused it with the interpretations of the ancient masters;
second, they lost the original intent of the "simultaneous roaming. As for the interpretation of the ancient masters, Zhanran (Zhang’an) refuted it, saying: "One bird exhausts its birth below."
The death of one bird represents the ultimate height of *nirvāṇa*, while the sinking of the other represents the eternal divergence from it; where, then, is their "flying together"?

Since you have identified *nirvāṇa* as principle (*li*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as phenomena (*shi*), it follows that one bird reaches the ultimate height and the other reaches the ultimate depth.

Thus, "flying together" cannot be established, which is precisely the point refuted by Zhāng'ān. Having reached the extremes of both height and depth, the original intent of "flying together"—which was fundamentally a metaphor—has been lost.
If the single essence and its characteristics are mutually identical, how can one take birth-and-death and nirvana as opposites to constitute "wandering in both"?

Furthermore, in three instances, Zhanran (Zhang’an) states that the two functions are simultaneously [identical to] the Middle, yet he takes the non-duality of the two truths and the Middle as the point where they are unified and return to the essence.
This would mean that half of the two functions must return to the essence, in which case the two functions could no longer be established.

Next, the present section is further divided into two parts: first, the correct elucidation; second, the resolution of doubts. The correct elucidation is further divided into five meanings: first, high and low; second, phenomena and principle;
third, wandering and resting; fourth, horizontal and vertical; fifth, ordinary beings and sages. Regarding the first meaning, as the commentary states:
"Both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa possess both the permanent and the impermanent; likewise, they exist both below and above, and one may wander or rest in either."
Regarding this cessation of birth and death and nirvāṇa, how are they distinguished? They do not differ in terms of delusion and awakening.
The nirvāṇa attained by the Tathāgata through awakening is superior, while the birth and death experienced by sentient beings while in delusion are inferior.
This is because the sutra specifically discusses the nirvāṇa of the three virtues as the fruit attained by the Tathāgata; it is the fruit that has been attained and realized.

The wondrous principle of the three virtues is fundamentally not a separate dharma; it points entirely to the very substance of the three paths of birth-and-death of sentient beings as being suchness itself.
If this is so, since birth-and-death and nirvana differ in terms of delusion and awakening, how can one see their mutual identity in their very substance?

One should know that the reason they are identical in substance is precisely because each possesses both the functions of permanence and impermanence; this is clarified through the distinction between the high and the low.
Thus they are established as each possessing [two functions]; yet, if we consider the meaning of their functional application, although each possesses two functions, their essence is identical.
To forcibly distinguish between delusion and awakening is fundamentally without basis. This means that the principle-essence of the three dharmas is without difference.

Having thus clarified their relative status, one first perceives the original essence in which both [principle and phenomenon] move together. Regarding the second point, the unity of phenomenon and principle, as the commentary states: "To take phenomena as principle."
Principle and phenomena are identical; the two truths are identical with the Middle, and the Middle is identical with the two truths.

It is not that there are two middles, yet within the two middles, the meaning of "traversing both" is established, and the analogy of the male and female is likewise established. As for how phenomena and principle are to be distinguished:

one should know that phenomena are the three thousand realms created by phenomena, while principle is the three thousand realms created by principle. Since these are precisely the dual creation of phenomena and principle, it is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
The recorded phenomena are dark, yet the principle is not dark; the manifestations are bright, yet the principle is not bright.
Although the positions of phenomenon and principle differ, they are said to be mutually non-obstructive because the dual movement of cause results in the dual movement of fruition.
Thus, practicing within what is not the Way is also like this. Once one has attained the realization of the phrase of "dual movement," the three thousand worlds are all termed "not the Way."
The delusion and craving shown [in the text] are not separate from emptiness; the principle of light and darkness is the same, and only then is it called the Buddha-way.
Speaking according to this passage, is it not the case that Jingxi took the two modes of creation (*zao*) to be precisely the meaning of "dual roaming" (*shuangyou*) between phenomena and principle?

Therefore, one should know that within the single *sanqian* (three thousand realms), whether high or low, dual roaming and simultaneous cessation are what Siming referred to as "mutually pervasive" and "mutually identical."
When these are gathered together, they mutually possess two functions; that is, the two modes of creation—phenomenal and principle—constitute the three thousand [dharmas].

Since these two modes of creation are themselves the three truths, there follows another set of two truths. Because the Middle is identical with the two truths, and the two truths are identical with the Middle, all dharmas—birth-and-death and nirvana—are each and every one none other than the three truths.
Because each and every one possesses them, there are the three thousand [dharmas] of the two modes of creation: phenomenal and principle.
Since the Middle and the Extremes are identical in essence and non-dual, even "oneness" cannot be established; therefore, the third stage is the simultaneous extinction and illumination of both.
Because the three truths are all extinguished, it is not the second stage. Although they are extinguished, there is illumination because the three truths are all illuminated;

thus, although there are these two stages regarding phenomena and principle within the second stage, these two subsequent stages do not go beyond the extinction and illumination of the Middle and the Extremes, despite there being three stages in total.

It is simply that regarding the phenomena and principle of the three truths (*triratna*), within the three thousand [dharmas] of the middle and the extremes, "extinguishing and illuminating" merely explains that the essence of the phenomena and principle is thus.
When these three truths are both extinguished and both illuminated, it is the same as what the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "The three truths have no form and are all invisible.

This means they are first simultaneously extinguished and then simultaneously illuminated. It is said that the provisional dharma (*prajñapti-dharma*) can be distinguished through phenomena; this refers precisely to this.

The provisional dharma is itself emptiness and itself the Middle; within emptiness and the Middle, the two essences are non-dual. The nature of the mind is unmoving, yet we provisionally establish the name "Middle";
when the three thousand realms are extinguished and vanish, we provisionally establish the designation "Emptiness. Though they vanish, they remain, and thus we provisionally establish these names.

This passage is identical to the simultaneous engagement with both the Middle and the non-Middle; while it is neither the Middle nor the non-Middle, it is both the Middle and the non-Middle. Only through such a single turn of dual function can one perceive their identity.
All phenomena pervade all places; there is no phenomenon that is not thus, and no phenomenon that cannot be so. Why?

Because they do not transcend the three thousand [realms] and the three truths. Regarding the third, "wandering and resting": "wandering" means wandering together, and "resting" means resting simultaneously.

As the commentary states: "Whether below or above, they wander together and rest simultaneously. Now, how can one discuss such matters as permanence and impermanence regarding these principles and phenomena?

Regarding "wandering and resting," one should know that when discussing their mutual identity (*sōjaku*) by correlating phenomena (*ji*) and principle (*ri*), the point of indicating this mutual identity through both the permanent and the impermanent is termed "wandering in tandem" (*sōyū*).
Since wandering in tandem is nothing other than mutual identity, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"Because the nature of reality and phenomena are mutually identical, it is called 'wandering in tandem,'" and further: "The meanings of the mutual identity of phenomena and principle do not obstruct one another."
It is said that the expression "flying together" (shuangyou) necessarily implies mutual identity; thus we know that "flying together" is simply a metaphor for "mutual identity.

What is termed "flying together" in the analogy is termed "mutual identity" in the principle (*dharma*). As for the simultaneous cessation [of their flight], since "flying together" is predicated upon mutual identity, one can thereby understand that "simultaneous cessation" refers to this.
This is discussed in terms of a single essence: the two birds flying together serve as a metaphor for the unity of phenomena and principle.
Generally speaking, because this is discussed in terms of a single dharma, it is illustrated by the metaphor of simultaneous rest;
because it is discussed in terms of two dharmas, it is illustrated by the metaphor of flying together. Although there are two birds, their resting and flying are never apart.

This skillful metaphor shows that phenomena and principle are of one essence and mutually identical; its subtlety is such as this. As Zhanran (Zhang’an) said: "The primary truth (paramārtha) is not permanent."
Because they are impermanent, there is no distinction between them. If the two birds fly together, it clarifies their dual function;
if the two birds both rest, it clarifies their mutual quiescence. To be quiescent through function—that is, for extinction to be bliss—is Great Nirvāṇa.
Since the text uses the ultimate truth of Great Nirvāṇa to discuss this simultaneous resting, is it not a single dharma discussed as a simultaneous cessation? If one attains this...

In the mind, the principle of the Middle Way is given the same name as its function, and thus one may naturally comprehend it. Regarding the fourth point on the horizontal and vertical [dimensions], as the commentary states:
"The horizontal and vertical are fully present without deficiency; how then are the horizontal and vertical to be distinguished?

One should know that the horizontal refers to phenomena (*dharma*), while the vertical refers to persons. This is because the three phases are of one essence and mutually identical, such that birth-and-death and nirvana are further...
Since there is no differentiation, how can one distinguish [the stages]? Therefore, it is necessary to rely on the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Whenever our school discusses the Mahāyāna sūtras regarding the point where birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, the single term "identical" (*ji*) must necessarily be distinguished;

for there are six levels of identity (*liu ji*). Thus, one must rely on the person. If one distinguishes by means of these six identities, as Jingxi [Zhanran] said: "How could it be that ignorance obstructs wisdom?"

Since they still exist without being destroyed and are named as such because light and darkness are mutually identical (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the principle for the practitioner of contemplation is likewise one of mutual identity.
How could one exclusively attribute this merit to a superior person? One should know that when discussing the vertical based on the horizontal, each [aspect] is fully present;

when discussing the horizontal based on the vertical, there is no deficiency. Thus, when discussing the horizontal based on the Dharma, although one simultaneously traverses both and brings both to rest, [the vertical remains].
Whether beings are upright—whether below or above—or horizontal, it is simply because their principle (*li*) is the same; even those who are upright differ only in terms of phenomena (*shi*).
Thus, the meanings of the six horizontal and the upright do not obstruct one another, for phenomena and principle have never for a moment been different.
Therefore, Jingxi said: "It deeply accords with the perfect purport and forever leaves behind all faults; this is truly due to this. Fifth, regarding ordinary beings and sages:

As the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "In this context, there are fully present those practiced by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) alone, those practiced by ordinary and noble ones (*ārya*) together, and those practiced neither by ordinary nor noble ones together;

these are all established through the distinction of persons and dharmas. Thus, while the preceding section clarified [the stages] vertically, which already pertained to the meaning of 'stages' (*avasthā*), why does it now again refer to ordinary and noble ones?
One should know that the bird metaphor in the Sūtra is precisely the answer to the question: 'How is one associated with the noble ones (*ārya*)?'"

The inquiry regarding their practice is already concise; by describing them as traveling together and resting side-by-side, it clarifies the reason for their joint practice. It must be discussed that ordinary beings and sages are equally so;

such "neither ordinary nor sage" refers to what was mentioned above as the identity of principle (*li*). As for "ordinary and sage," this refers to what was mentioned above as the difference in phenomena (*shi*).
The distinction between ordinary and sage is made based on delusion and awakening, while the selection of horizontal and vertical is made based on the universal application of cause and effect.
Regarding the general selection (*sāmānya-vicāra*), our school generally selects from among all Mahāyāna sūtras;

specifically, as for the selection based on the differentiation of dharmas within those sūtras, although the intentions expressed therein differ according to the distinctions between ordinary beings and sages, or delusion and awakening, the essence of the dharma (*dharma-tattva*) has never been different.
This "simultaneous roaming and concurrent cessation" is precisely the original intent of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in its discourse on the eternal (*nitya*).

The general outline consists of five points of differing meaning, all of which are based on a single passage from the original commentary on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* to expound the great principles of *nirvāṇa* in this manner.

Regarding the resolution of doubts, there are briefly five layers: first, resolving the doubt that [the teaching] applies exclusively to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; second, resolving the doubt regarding the lack of... [the creation by phenomena].

1. Resolving doubts regarding permanence; 2. Resolving doubts regarding the principle that gives rise to function; 3. Resolving doubts regarding the universal application of the sections across other teachings; 4. Resolving doubts regarding the two functions of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Regarding the first [doubt]:

Now we ask, since there is not one among the various Mahāyāna sūtras of the single lifetime [of the Buddha] that does not discuss [the identity of essence and function], for what reason are these two functions found only in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*? One should know that this is merely a difference in textual expression.

The reason this scripture is distinguished by its textual title is precisely because it correctly discourses upon the eternal (*nitya*). As Jingxi stated: "The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* upholds the rules of discipline (*vinaya*) to manifest the eternal.

Furthermore, as the *Miaoxuan* says, it is called "discoursing on the eternal" and "discerning the nature" (*dhātu*). If, however, the eternal were used to refute the impermanent (*anitya*), that would be a remedial teaching (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) rather than the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
As the Commentary states: "The two birds flying together is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s non-duality."
Regarding the two functions, the *Śāstra* explains that permanence and impermanence are counteractive dharmas and not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
However, what is clarified here regarding the Tathāgata’s non-dual dual function is that he is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet he can manifest both permanence and impermanence;

this is identical to the section on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If explained in terms of the provisional and the real according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or in terms of permanence and impermanence according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, [the meaning remains the same].
Although the teachings differ according to various conditions, their underlying Dharma-principle remains the same; though the paths diverge, they lead to the same destination.

Expedient means (*upāya*) and ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), permanence and impermanence, are merely different names for the same source. If one were to refute impermanence by means of permanence, it would be identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s judgment that the Way is not distinct from impermanence.
Therefore, if the primary truth (*paramārtha*) is neither permanent nor impermanent, it is capable of being permanent.

If one can understand impermanence as being identical to the meaning of "opening" [the provisional] as found in the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is as the commentary states: "Opening the former impermanence is precisely the present permanence.
When explained in this way, the text concerning these two functions is distinct from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* regarding the teachings of the past. Why is this?

Because the teachings of the past had not yet been opened and revealed. If one does not clarify permanence by means of this opening and revealing, but instead directly relies on the single essence where the aspects are mutually identical, that is the perfect permanence.
To explain this principle, it is somewhat consistent with various Mahāyāna sūtras. Regarding the resolution of the second layer of doubt:

we now ask, if the phenomenal creation (*shizao*) were impermanent, it would be exactly like the view refuted by Jingjue. Since Jingjue correctly employs this very text [of the *Fahua wenju*], how can one know this?
As the *Yi bian* (Compilation on Meaning) cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, which takes the "three thousand realms" to be the emptiness that is not the path (*feidao kong*).
Regarding the path of the Buddha, it is said that one should entrust this to later students and reflect deeply upon these words;

in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, it is precisely because the Buddha-path is not a [conventional] path that one dwells in the duality of movement and stillness (*yì*). If this were the case, then phenomena would be impermanent, which would accord with the Pure Awakening’s view of taking the three thousand [realms] as that which is to be destroyed.
One should know that this is not so; rather, these two functions here precisely manifest that in the Four Ming [teachings], phenomena and principle are one.
Since the essence and its attributes are identical, how could there be impermanence as something subject to refutation? Now, these two functions are already one in their identity;
impermanence is entirely identical to permanence. Only when not moving from a single dharma do we see the two functions both manifesting and simultaneously ceasing.

If, however, one were to refute phenomena to reveal principle, this would directly contradict the two functions; thus, the simultaneous manifestation of both would be entirely unestablished, as in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) where it refutes [the notion of] destruction.
The ancients called this "a single wheel and a solitary wing," unable to fly or transport itself;

it is precisely for this reason that one must thoroughly understand the identity of the three truths—the principles of the permanent and the impermanent—and their mutual interpenetration whether in the lower or the higher realms, where every phenomenon remains distinct yet perfectly integrated.
If one does not personally realize this meaning, how could one avoid being deluded by the biased interpretations of Jingjue? How then could one fully perceive the errors of others?
To clarify deeply the meaning of the identity of the perfect [nature], the third layer of doubt is now addressed by asking Jingxi:

"The essence of principle (li-ti) is without differentiation; how then can differentiation be attributed to its phenomenal function (shi-yong)? Furthermore, the 'principle-creation' (li-zao) explained here belongs entirely to function;
whether it be phenomenon or principle, both are termed 'function. This question has persisted for a long time and may also be expanded into two parts."
