"The ordinary and the sage are one as form and fragrance are extinguished in purity"—these two phrases illustrate, respectively, the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*), showing that the environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely contained within the self-mind of the most supreme Sage;
"the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed a single thought-moment of the lowest ordinary being"—these two phrases illustrate the mutual fusion of cause and effect.
The intent of the first phrase encompasses the nine realms of existence, yet it cites the most inferior state of suffering as an example.
The nine realms are precisely the Buddha-realm. Allow me to attempt a discussion on this: this single phrase alone is sufficient to sweep away heterodox paths and clear the orthodox Way.
Why is this so? From the Avīci hell—the lowest realm of suffering for both the environment and its inhabitants—to the dung beetle class, is it not likewise so?

They are all entirely within the self-mind of the ultimate Sage; they are the ultimate identity (*tathatā*). Since this is so at the level of ultimate reality, it is likewise so at the levels of partial realization and so forth.

Is this not indeed so? If you claim that the current text merely reveals nature (*xing*) and does not reveal phenomena (*xiang*), why then does it specifically state that "the environment and inhabitants of Avīci are perfectly perceived, and principle and phenomena are fully present in a single thought-moment"? Are the environment and inhabitants of Avīci not the creation of phenomena (*shi-zao*)?
If you have faith in Jingxi [Zhiyi], how can you not believe Siming [Zhili]? As for the statement that "when the fruit is realized, all ten [realms] are ultimate," [it follows accordingly].
As for the second phrase, the fruit of Buddhahood is precisely the nine realms. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Since the ten realms, along with their environments and inhabitants, causes and effects, are thus mutually fused, this is precisely the wondrous Dharma of the Three Thousand.
Therefore, one should know that these four phrases alone are sufficient to demonstrate the Three Thousand wondrous objects of contemplation within the mind that contemplates.

Once the wondrous realm is established, Buddha-nature is naturally all-pervasive; it is not the case that Buddha-nature is not pervasive according to other schools, which posit that the sentient and the insentient share a single substance.
This is precisely the meaning shown in the "Exemplification of the Inconceivable Realm" (*Yìlì*) as being distinct from what others establish; it begins by stating:
"Because the Buddha-vehicle is established within the insentient realm. The general purport of the *Jīnbí* lies entirely herein. Below:
In expounding this teaching, one does not depart from these three thousand wonderful realms within a single thought-moment.

If even the text of the *Golden Needle* in its single scroll should be set aside as a provisional method (*dharma*), how much more so that which is not the Dharma? Now, establishing that the essence of the true cause (*tathāgata-garbha*) of sentient beings is all-pervasive, the scriptural text likewise uses empty space as a metaphor;
this accords with the provisional teachings (*upāya*) contained within the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. However, if we rely on the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), it should be stated thus:

Now, regarding the establishment of the three causes for sentient beings as being pervasive in substance, other schools merely believe that sentient beings possess the direct cause of Buddha-nature within their minds;
they do not believe it is pervasive throughout insentient things, and thus claim that insentient things lack Buddha-nature.

As clarified here, the initial mind of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is said to be "restricted," even when hearing the truth: it is restricted to the mind capable of creating [retribution]. Furthermore, as the text says: "If..."

The Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) truly states that the three principles are fundamentally pervasive; it further says, "In order to show sentient beings their originally existing correct nature, one speaks of 'correct pervasiveness' (zhengbian)," yet this does not clarify the text.

How, then, can one distinguish between the Separate and Complete [teachings] regarding the cultivation and nature? One should know that the distinction between the Separate and Complete was personally clarified by Jingxi [Zhiyi];
the difference lies solely in whether they are distinct or identical. Therefore, various Mahāyāna sūtras may state that sentient beings are originally...

There is the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*), or it is said that sentient beings fundamentally possess three causes; the distinction between the Separate (*pratyekabuddha*) and Perfect (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) lies solely in whether these are identical or non-identical.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* merely speaks of the "correct and universal," which is still a discourse on the Real (*satya*) while retaining the provisional (*upāya*). If one were to directly rely on the provisional alone, even what is "correct" would be limited.

One should know that in the Separate Teaching, the stages prior to the ground (*bhūmi*) and those on the ground are contrasted such that the nine are destroyed to reveal the one; for this reason, some say there is only one [cause].

Regarding the nature (*prakṛti*), it is not said that the nature possesses three causes. If one refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), because the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the initial arousal of the mind have already subsumed the nature through cultivation, it is therefore also called "one nature.

In reality, although the three dharmas of cause and effect, and cultivation and nature, differ between the Separate and Perfect Teachings—being either identical or non-identical—their doctrinal tenets are distinct.
Since the Separate Teaching maintains that they are "non-identical," all three dharmas therein belong [to the category of being distinct].
Regarding the reason why Jingxi established three kinds of Buddha-realms, the Perfect [teaching] is not like this, for there is nothing that is not the Buddha-realm.
I address these words to students: you must pay close attention to the three dharmas of the causal realm of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings], namely cultivation and nature.

A former sage said, "To learn without reflecting leads to confusion," and a predecessor of antiquity further remarked, "The difficulty in contemplating meaning lies in its lack of clarity; one should reflect thoroughly until it becomes clear."
The three dharmas elucidated here in this distinct teaching (biejiao) may be compared to obtaining a balance scale and a ruler;
with them, one can fully know the long and short, the heavy and light, throughout the world.

Regarding the division of the teachings into Great and Small—whether referred to as "Treasury and Perfect" (zangyuan) or "Partial and Perfect" (pianyuan)—none of these fail to comprehend the refutations and establishments within this [teaching].

The underlying intent here differs from that of the *Fuxing*. Now, following the questioner’s inquiry, I shall first explain the meaning of the four teachings according to what our Master Ren (Jingci) takes as his primary authority.
Previously, Jingci broadly categorized the various volumes of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures, contrasting the provisional and the real within the Great Sūtras;

this was not yet a specialized analysis of the doctrinal meanings of our own school’s teachings. One should know that in the preceding text, whenever "Mahāyāna" and "Hīnayāna" were mentioned, it referred only to the categories of the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*).

If one were to categorize and divide [the teachings] directly according to the meanings of the *Zangyuan* (Treasury of the Perfect) and other such works, although the meaning of insentient things possessing Buddha-nature as expounded in various Mahāyāna sūtras ultimately converges upon the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), one must not immediately employ the specific doctrinal tenets of our own school to debate against other schools.
Rather, one may only debate by generally synthesizing the various Mahāyāna sūtras in contrast with the sūtras of the Śrāvaka Hīnayāna schools. If...

Regarding the fact that in the Great Teachings (Mahāyāna) the conditions and causes (*pratyaya* and *hetu*) are not universal, this is because they represent the provisional (*upāya*) while teaching the real (*bhūta*).

Thus, one knows that other schools fail to understand the relative scale of the teachings, and even within the Great Teachings, they fail to discern the passages concerning the provisional and the real.
I have frequently observed scholars who do not yet understand the meaning of the relative scale of these scriptural collections; I urge you to search through them all.

What our own school has taught is now proven to have its proper destination. This "Exegesis on the Ten Meanings" (*Fuxing*) evaluates matters according to the doctrines of our own school, intending to ensure that students of our tradition have no confusion regarding the underlying principle.
Although Jingxi [Zhiyi] composed the *Golden Scalpel* (*Jinbi*) to point the way, he feared that students might still not fully understand;
thus, he again evaluated the matter through the text concerning "color and fragrance" using these ten meanings, in accordance with the teachings.

In establishing a single principle against rival schools, one must understand that the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) provides a comprehensive analysis by integrating the provisional and the real across both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions;
whereas the *Fuxing* (Aids to Practice) offers a specific evaluation based solely on the doctrines of our own school.
Thus, those who study within our tradition today each have their respective points of reference and should not be treated as interchangeable.
One should know that all phenomena are True Suchness because they do not change; and that True Suchness is all phenomena because it follows conditions.
This is thus using the terminology employed by other schools to demonstrate that Buddha-nature is entirely True Suchness following conditions.
What could the term "all phenomena" possibly exclude? Are form and mind separated from it? Buddha-nature and True Suchness are merely different names for one and the same reality.
The reason [the Master] immediately rebuts you by saying, "If you truly believe that insentient things lack Buddha-nature, does this not mean that the myriad dharmas lack True Suchness?

The analogy of waves and water illustrates the nature of dharmas; it should be understood that when our school’s master Jingxi speaks extensively of "following conditions" (*suiyuan*), he does not go beyond this meaning.
If one establishes the Buddha-nature of insentient things based on "following conditions," yet fails to explain "inherent possession" (*ju*), such an establishment cannot be maintained.

As for how the Perfect and Separate Teachings might be reconciled, why is it that this text focuses exclusively on demonstrating the universality of Buddha-nature by means of "following conditions" (*suiyuan*)?

Even if one were to interpret the meaning according to each school’s own doctrine without conflict—such that the Separate Teaching also establishes "following conditions"—it remains the case that the Patriarch [Zhiyi] has not yet been seen to provide explicit proof.

All the passages cited here concern the "arising" (*sheng*) of phenomena; I venture to say that the *Sijiaoyi zhizhang* (The Essential Meaning of the Four Teachings) by Siming [Zhiyun] is the definitive guide.
Although you, of the River Qiáo, alone have supported and established this position, I have scrutinized the *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) and do not yet dare to accept its authority.

As for the meaning of "words" (*zi*) as the perfect expression (*yuanquan*) of all phenomena—a sublime song from the Mountain School (Shan-jia)—this is not what is being discussed here. It is truly laughable that you, of the River Qiáo, are so preoccupied with right and wrong.
Furthermore, your attempt to verify the current refutation by citing the passage on the "partial True Suchness" (*fen zhenru*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is misplaced.
It is clear that this "Worthy Leader" (Xian-shou) merely refutes the Worthy Leader; others have transmitted this by hearsay.

Scholars of other schools take the forty-two characters of our own school’s system of correspondence as their model, intending thereby to rescue the passage on the "divided True Suchness" cited in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.

They argue that although this specific text does not appear within the one hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is not necessarily absent, given that the text has been abbreviated ninefold.

If it is argued that the "ninefold reduction" (jiubai lüqu) must necessarily be absent, why then does Tiantai’s forty-two characters correspond to the positions where the ninefold reduction must necessarily be present?
Now, I say there is both affirmation and negation. If one affirms its presence, it is as Jingxi did when he broadly provided a general explanation;
this is merely to be confused by the name while failing to understand the meaning. However, if one speaks from the perspective of negation, even though...
If one were to omit nine levels from the forty-two characters by way of abbreviation, such a correspondence would necessarily be impossible. Why?

Although there is no explicit text for these forty-two characters within the hundred fascicles of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when one examines and verifies their positions and meanings through various Mahāyāna sūtras, it is proven that the principle of nine levels must indeed exist.
How could one divide True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Having already divided True Suchness... [text ends].

Regarding the claim that the two schools differ in their understanding of the essence of *dharmatā* and *buddhadhātu* and thus hold different names for them—having examined and verified this against the various *Avataṃsaka* sūtras, it is certain that such a meaning does not exist therein.
Therefore, one should know through investigation that the principle of the "ninefold increase" (*kūgu*) is necessarily non-existent; of this there is no doubt.
Although this [error] was already a deviation propagated by other schools, later students have surreptitiously read the examples cited in our own school’s doctrinal sections to provide a defense.
The commentary on the *Awakening of Faith* must be analyzed with care; just as the meaning of translated scriptures must be verified by cross-referencing them against various sutras,

if one were to trust the passages cited in that commentary, one would have to divide the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) of the *Avataṃsaka* and other Mahayana sutras into two separate lineages.

The term "Buddha-nature" (foxing) has two meanings: first, the nature of all Buddhas pervades the minds of all sentient beings; second, the minds of all sentient beings pervade the nature of all Buddhas.
Although cause and effect follow different paths, they both ultimately converge in Buddha-nature, which never undergoes differentiation.
As the text says: "The Buddha is one who has attained the fruit; all sentient beings possess the nature of that fruit. This refers to the following.
This means that the Buddha-nature of all Buddhas pervades the minds of sentient beings. The text states: "Because the mind of afflictions pervades, it is said that Buddha-nature pervades.

This refers to the fact that the minds of sentient beings pervade the Buddha-natures of all Buddhas. Since the essence of the mind-nature is already all-pervasive, how could it be restricted to those who possess sentience?
If it were restricted to those with sentience, how could all Buddhas achieve enlightenment? [The text continues: "Because the rustic guest does not know."
Because of the meaning of the mind’s pervasiveness, one does not realize that matter (*rūpa*) is pervasive. If one knows that the mind is pervasive, why doubt that matter is pervasive?

Why is this so? Because the mind, matter, and Buddha-nature are but a single essence. Yet, while various texts—and those within this very work—often speak of "the mind creating" (*citta-kṛta*), they specifically mention matter.
This is because matter is itself the mind; thus, Guishan exclusively adheres to this point and the *Dà-yì* (Great Meaning), asserting that matter arises from...
The two lines, "The mind creates the whole body; all is the mind," mean that external forms do not inherently possess the three thousand realms and must therefore be subsumed within the mind.
This is because Jingxi [Zhiyi] intended to point out the meaning of "the mind creates" and "mind-only" as found in various Mahāyāna sūtras.
For the Mahāyāna generally speaks of "the mind creates" and "mind-only"; since form is identical to mind, both form and mind are all-pervasive.
If one does not believe that form pervades the mind, then form is separated from the mind and likewise does not pervade it. As Jingxi said: "It is restricted to me;

Śākyamuni exists only within the substance of the five aggregates. One should know that when various Mahāyāna sūtras speak of "creating," "possessing," "pervading," or "only" with respect to these meanings, one cannot further divide mind and form.
What need is there to wait for form to be subsumed into the mind before it can be "complete"? It is simply that...
Mahāyāna sūtras frequently speak of "mind" (*citta*) because they point it out as the fundamental basis for sentient beings' delusion and the source from which phenomena are created.

Siming said: "To use the easy to explain the difficult by taking mind as an analogy for form may not yet remove the doubts of students, nor may it resolve the arguments of Gushan. As for Siming’s establishment of the creation of mind and form:

The meaning of this [concept of] "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) is already perfectly and subtly exhausted; how could anything further be added? It merely serves to clarify the various texts. Master Xinzao says:

"That which is easy to understand must be examined with great care; it is not for students to remain unclear about this. If the *pariṇirmita* (retributive) environment is created collectively and the *sambhogika* (experiential) body is created individually, how can one believe that the collective is pervasive while disbelieving that the individual is pervasive? Since both the creator and the created are nothing but mind, [the principle applies equally].

Because the essence [of mind] cannot be restricted to a specific location, and because other schools clarify that all shared and individual retributive environments (*pratyaya*) are collectively produced by consciousness alone, they speak of "believing in common pervasiveness.
This is not because they do not believe in the individual pervasiveness [of the mind], but rather because they do not understand that the mind is pervasive;
thus, they hold that "all is consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Therefore, it is said: "How can one believe in common pervasiveness while disbelieving in individual pervasiveness? Indeed.

The subsequent summary demonstrates that both the creator (the primary elements) and the created (the derivative elements) are but mind; this is the mind of affliction. How could one seek an inconceivable realm apart from the aggregates and their objects?
Regarding the term "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), how could it refer solely to the True Mind? Why do you not see the explicit text of Jingxi [Zhiyi], which says:

"Discerning separately is to see the arising and ceasing of before and after; perfect discernment is to see that phenomena and principle are fully present within a single thought-moment. You must study this.
Those who do not know what the face of the afflictive mind actually looks like fall into biased interpretations;
they still claim that one must simply contemplate the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), yet they do not know where to discard the afflictions, nor where to seek the inconceivable.
You should know that what is called "inconceivable" is merely an empty fist. I constantly advise students not to give rise to frivolous theorizing (*prapañca*) and not to grasp at fragments.

One must certainly grasp the meaning; if one grasps the meaning, how could the words themselves be difficult? Furthermore, the reason they are difficult is truly because the meaning is not understood.
I observe that from antiquity, people have been driven by names and phrases.

For instance, the fact that since ancient times the "Buddha-nature of the insentient" has been suspected as a difficult matter is simply because the character "Buddha" was placed upon the name. You should know this.
The reason for speaking of it in this partial manner is to cause sentient beings to transform their delusion. As the text says:

"By showing that afflictions and birth-and-death are the Buddha-nature, one causes them to practice; this is called 'Buddha-nature. If one transforms one's own delusion, who would say there is no Buddha-nature?
Furthermore, the intention behind saying that [sentient beings] "possess" the nature is also like this; you should reflect upon this well.
One should know that sentient beings possess only principle, while the Buddhas possess phenomena; sentient beings realize principle, whereas the Buddhas realize phenomena.

Thus, although sentient beings have only the phenomena and principle within delusion, and the Buddhas possess both the phenomena and principle within awakening, though delusion and awakening differ, the essence of phenomena and principle is one.
This is also as stated in the *Miaoxuan*: "Sentient beings attain phenomena; sages attain principle. Furthermore—

The Sage attains the principle within phenomena, while the ordinary person attains the phenomena within the principle. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) explains: "Sentient beings attain that which is the phenomenon of the principle;
the Sage attains that which is the principle of the phenomenon. What the Sage knows, sentient beings do not know.

While the Sage attains matters such as cause and effect, the transformation of others, and responsive resonance, sentient beings only attain the principle within delusion—that which is neither cause nor effect. However, all...

The reason why the Buddha and sentient beings are discussed through the mutual interplay of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*) is that phenomena involve delusion and enlightenment, while principle involves cultivation and nature.

Although there are distinctions between delusion and enlightenment, as well as cultivation and nature, they do not transcend the "ten realms and a thousand suchnesses" (*bai jie qian ru*). Within a single mind or a single speck of dust, there is no place that does not inherently possess the three thousand [realms].
Sentient beings have not only failed to awaken; they are even unaware of their own delusion. Therefore, it is said: "Only... (referring to the Buddha).

There are phenomena and principles within delusion; the Buddhas have not only awakened to them, but have also revealed delusion itself—thus it is said that they possess both the phenomena and principles within awakening.
Students should know that, ultimately, all dharmas have never been subject to delusion or awakening; one does not know by what means to define delusion or awakening.
Furthermore, although the nature of sentient beings inherently possesses delusion, as long as they have not yet begun cultivation, they will naturally engage in self-discrimination.
The latter five [levels] differ from this; that is, the single phrase "Identity with Principle" (*li-ji*) is sufficient to manifest the distinctness of phenomena.

Why is it that our school establishes the term "Identity with Principle" to perfectly and completely explain all dharmas? It is because it refers entirely to the identity of the three paths with the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

Although one has not yet initiated practice, it serves as the foundation for the virtues of practice; because practice has not yet been initiated at all, Siming said: "This is the ultimate degree of disparagement."

This is because it is intended for students to know how to initiate cultivation. Since sentient beings have never been separated from discursive thought since beginningless time, the initial mind that initiates cultivation cannot be pointed to as being exclusively *tathatā* (suchness).
However, one must not simply follow the teachings of Siming [Zhiyi] either; nor should one force oneself to believe them.

One must instead gain a profound understanding of the intent of our own school’s doctrinal division (*jiaobu*). This is indeed the path by which the Buddhas of the ten directions transcend birth and death; it is truly fortunate.
It would be well to abandon contention and strive for liberation.

Regarding the "Ten Gates of Non-duality" in the *Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning* (*Shu-chi*), the section on the non-duality of matter and mind states: "In general, they are unified within a single thought-moment; in detail, they are distinguished as matter and mind."

The two dharmas of form and mind encompass all three thousand phenomena; these three thousand phenomena are themselves the gate of non-duality, precisely because each and every instance of form and mind is fully endowed [with the three thousand].

Although the Master of the House (Zhiyi) did not fail to indicate this principle of "endowment" within his various teachings, and although the Patriarch Siming (Zhiyuan) did not fail to clarify it through his ancestral transmission, such was the case that a biased interpretation first arose at the forefront and has been followed by tradition down to the present day.
Those who find errors here might later compose their own harmonizations, fearing that they would mislead future generations and cause them to slander the Dharma and give rise to dogmatic views;

I wish there were no need for such excuses, yet it seems impossible to avoid them. One should know that in the *Sèxīn bù'èr mén* (The Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind), Jingxi states: "To say they are 'all contained within a single thought' is the general principle;

to distinguish them as 'matter and mind' is the specific analysis. This was intended at the time to point out that within the wondrous matter and mind of the objective realm (*ālambana*), all phenomena are fully present—this is the meaning of *mahā*.
Śamatha and vipaśyanā together constitute this "one thought-moment as the three thousand [realms]"—the inconceivable object.

However, it is only in the present text that these are explained through the ten profundities (*daśamithyā*) to clarify the dharmas subsumed within the exegesis. Therefore, a general and specific exposition is employed: taking up a single dharma, one shows that it encompasses all dharmas.
Since a single dharma can encompass all dharmas, that which is capable of encompassing them is termed the "general" (*sāmānya*), while those which are encompassed are the "specific" (*viśeṣa*).

All dharmas are designated as "particulars," while the "universal" is that which is able to encompass them; the "particular" is that which is encompassed. The single term "universal" is itself a particular name for that which encompasses.

One must not become confused by the names and thereby lose the great essence. According to the teachings of the Shanjia (Mount Siming) school, the Dharma of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-quan*) of the One Vehicle is such that each and every thing is complete within it.
Thus, phenomenon and principle share the same substance; even when one dharma is raised, there is nothing outside of this one dharma.

There is no other dharma such that if there were another dharma, its phenomena and principle would differ in essence and thus fail to be a perfect expression. To cite a phenomenon is itself the principle;

to cite the principle is itself the phenomenon. How could one forcibly divide them? That the principle exists while phenomena do not, or that one divides phenomena and principle, belongs to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

Thus we know that the reason the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) distinguishes among all dharmas is for the sake of the perfect and the partial, in order to cause those who are deluded to transform their confusion. If it were only...

The perfect expression [of reality] is but a single *dharmatā*; how could there be two? That being so, when all phenomena (*dharmas*) are perfectly expressed, each phenomenon serves as the "total" (*sāmānya*) and each phenomenon serves as the "particular" (*viśeṣa*).
Why is this? Because all phenomena are fully present within one another. As for why the present text points specifically to "one thought-moment," it is as Siming said:
"If one discusses the mutual inclusion of all phenomena, then whichever single phenomenon is raised may serve as the 'total'; thus, the three [natures] are without difference."

Furthermore, because it is now intended for ease of contemplation, a single thought-moment of mind is pointed out as the "total" (the universal). However, one must understand that this total and its particulars cannot be separated;

they correspond respectively to principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). Principle inherently possesses the three thousand [realms], and the phenomenal function of the three thousand each has its own total and particulars.

Only when these two aspects are mutually identical can they be called the "wondrous realm. This is the outstanding achievement of Siming in the Shanjia tradition, by which he attained the essence of the doctrinal sections.

I consider that since the *Mohe zhiguan* takes this entirety of form and mind as the inconceivable object (*asambhava-viṣaya*), it is precisely what is meant by "the three thousand in a single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa-trisāhasra*).
Thus, if one refers to the present text, it is called "totality within a single thought-moment"; if one refers to the *Zhiguan*, it is called "the three thousand in a single thought-moment.

This "single thought-moment" is the very substance of the objects of the aggregates (*skandha-viṣaya*), specifically identified as the "single thought-moment" that constitutes the essence of the objects.

How could one seek the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) elsewhere? Furthermore, as the *Dayi* (Great Meaning) says: "Because it does not change while following conditions, it is called 'nature' (xing);
because it changes while following conditions, it is called 'mind' (xin). If [the mind] does not pertain to phenomena (dharma), to what dharma would it pertain?

If it pertains to phenomena, why do you not believe in the fourfold and singlefold aspects of phenomena as taught by Zhiyi (Sima Ming)? If you do believe in the singlefold and manifold aspects of phenomena, then phenomena and principle (li) are of the same essence, and every dharma is all-encompassing.
What doubt could there possibly be? Master Jingxi’s clarity and brilliance are like the sun and moon; why, then, do you still ask from which text it originates?
Take, for example, the "three thousand wondrous realms" originating from the text of the *Lotus Sūtra*—how could there not be such words as "three thousand"?

Moreover, they are all subsumed within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), and that this single thought-moment pertains to phenomena is extremely easy to understand. In the present text, since this single thought-moment is precisely [the reality]...

In the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the phrase "the mind creates" (*xin-zao*) is cited from the text and elucidated by Jingxi as being twofold: first, in terms of principle (*li*), and second, in terms of phenomena (*shi*).

The perfect vision of both phenomena and principle is fully present within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). The phenomena of this single thought-moment are, in their very essence, identical to principle;

for, as the subsequent text explains, all particular phenomena are subsumed into the universal, such that there is not a single dharma that is not the nature of mind—a single nature that is itself without nature.

The three thousand [realms] appear vividly; it is said that there is nothing that is not the nature of mind. This "single nature which is no-nature" means that when a single thought is free from transgression, it is immediately the principle (*li*).
That "the three thousand appear vividly" means that phenomena (*shi*) and principle are of the same substance and are fully present therein.

Why then do we say that principle is "comprehensive" while phenomena are "distinct"? To point out the essential: the "comprehensiveness" of phenomena refers to their totality within a single thought-moment, while their "distinction" refers to the differentiation of form and mind. This is the principle.

Regarding "the general and the specific," this refers to the principle (li) creating the three thousand realms. Since phenomenon and principle are mutually identical and cannot be divided or opposed, if one were to say that the principle is general while phenomena are specific, one must ask:
from what text does this derive? If this is not a heterodox interpretation, what kind of comprehensive insight is it?
Since the time of Nanping, successive masters of the past have rejected and refuted this view; there is no scholar who has not [done so].
Believing and accepting the Way of the Four Illuminations, when the predecessors had passed away, those who were errant and deluded acted again, claiming to be the sole authority in the East.

Su Dongpo said: "This culture has become a heterodox teaching; as for scholars employing barbarians, gentlemen find no way to do good with them, while petty men flow along with them, believing they have found their time.
It is like a deep mountain or vast marsh where the dragons and tigers have vanished."
The passing away and transformation of nature manifest in a hundred ways; eels and eels dance while foxes and badgers howl—these words exhaust the matter.
They exhaust it! Alas!
This is the three thousand books of Master Yue’s Discernment.

Master Yue’s *Three Thousand Writings* (Sānqiānshū) refutes Siming, stating: "The Dharma-gate realized throughout the Great Master’s life does not transcend what is called the three thousand [realms] within the mundane world.
Thus, in the two volumes of his *Pointers to the Essentials* (*Zhǐyào*), totaling forty-two sheets, there are more than one hundred and fifty instances where he speaks of the "three thousand.
Observing Master Yue’s appraisal so thoroughly, it appears he intended to disparage [the other].

Why is this praised? It is because Siming took the "Three Thousand" as the dharma-gate of what is realized—the direct lineage of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation)—wherein the inconceivable realm of "the three thousand in a single thought-moment" is entirely the practice of one's own mind according to Tiantai.

Thus, the phenomena of the ten realms, the ten suchnesses, and the three types of worlds, including all causes and effects, are none other than the mutual inclusion and mutual fusion of the three truths.
The hundred realms and thousand suchnesses constitute the three thousand worlds; since one world is itself the three thousand worlds, what hindrance is there in naming the three thousand "the world"?
The differentiation of the three thousand worlds is non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is differentiation; they are a single essence through mutual identity. Why is this?
Because there is not a single dharma that is not the three truths. How could one, upon merely hearing the name "world," [fail to realize this]?

O Bhayānaka, I shall now test you with a question: If you maintain that the mundane world consists of differentiated phenomena, then since these differentiations are limited to the ten realms, how could they possibly constitute the "thousand suchnesses" within the hundred realms?
It must be that the causal and resultant distinctions of the ten realms, in their very place, are entirely and non-dually the Three Truths;
because each and every one is mutually inclusive and mutually interfused, they constitute the "three thousand [realms]," which is the name for this.

Regarding the "Inconceivable Realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*) and the Tiantai school’s teaching on the perfect three truths (*triratna-satya*): they are neither identical nor different, for they constitute a single essence.
Consequently, their distinction and non-distinction cannot be definitively categorized as opposing attributes. This principle is easy to understand;

however, because students fail to find the door by which to enter it, they consequently suspect it to be difficult to comprehend. The *Jiyao* (Essential Points) explains this through the ten non-dualities (*daśādvaya*), clarifying the objective realm.

The *Myōkōshaku* (Exposition on the Ten Subtleties) clarifies that the dharmas of cause and effect, self and other, which it explicates, ultimately point toward the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Great Calming and Contemplation), where the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" (*ichinen sanzen*) is the ultimate destination.

Thus it says: "Throughout the entire span of existence, whether vertical or horizontal, nothing transcends the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment; the mundane world is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Master Jingxi’s clear and explicit instructions show that within each of the ten gates, every dharma is the three thousand realms. How could one not marvel that the *Shiyao* (Essential Points) contains forty-two pages [of this teaching]?
The mention of the "three thousand [dharmas]" in more than one hundred and fifty places is precisely because Siming deeply grasped the intent of Jingxi;

thus, he was able to compose this commentary. Throughout, Siming points out the three thousand dharmas as if observing the great movements from the pivot of the celestial sphere, or discerning the future from the essential principles of the present.
The *Shuji* states that in the *Fuxing*, it is clearly explained that both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) take the "three thousand [realms]" as their guiding principle.

Consequently, one recognizes the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as necessarily requiring the presence of the three thousand; yet, one fails to realize that these are the phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) inherent within the nature of the mind.

This is because, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the intention behind "opening up the provisional to reveal the real" lies in the provisional itself; therefore, the three thousand are not discussed when opening up the provisional.

If one does not survey the three thousand realms of the enlightened environment and beings, one’s illumination of the objective field will necessarily be incomplete; it is essential to examine thoroughly the causes and effects, the self and others, and the primary and secondary worlds.
To contemplate these within one's own mind is precisely the intended meaning of this "Guiding Manual."
Bian said: What I now call the "guiding principle" refers to its essential point. Because the three thousand realms share one and the same nature, there is only the One Dharma;

because there is only the One Dharma, it possesses the wondrous realm of the three thousand in a single thought-moment. Furthermore, this emerges from the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) as the true lineage.
The *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies the provisional and the real, the primary essence, and correctly elucidates the method of contemplation, taking this very principle as its ultimate consummation.

Regarding the ultimate and most profound teaching, if one claims that it is intended to universally encompass cause and effect, self and others, the environment and its inhabitants, and that one should regard one’s own mind as the guiding compass, then this is a case of being lost as to where the compass itself lies. It seems Master En no Gyoja was merely seeking his own pleasure;
he has betrayed the teachings and deceived future generations to such an extent. Furthermore, he clings to the notion that the Three Thousand Worlds are the nature of the mind.
Regarding that which possesses the dharmas of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): the conventional truth consists of the three thousand [realms] as phenomenal creation;

this phenomenal creation of the three thousand is itself the three thousand as ontological principle (*li*). Only when phenomenon and principle are one body does the meaning of "complete possession" truly come to be established within the single mind.

Who could distinguish between phenomenon and principle? It is because Master Yue failed to clarify the meaning of the character "immediately" (*ji*) that he produced such a perverse interpretation; in reality, there was no such thing.
He also once said to scholars: "Master Yue was a man of outstanding intelligence; were he not one who had clearly realized the teachings, how could he have produced such a deviant interpretation?

How tragic that this 'cutting off of the three thousand'—which belongs to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as inherent within the nature and mind—has led some people to this day to still propagate it as a common saying, despite its errors."
That is to say, regarding the Tiantai school’s doctrine of the three thousand realms and the three truths, such an explanation must be made.

In principle there is nothing, while in phenomena everything exists; this is entirely identical to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Furthermore, in the *Yibian*, it states that the three thousand realms are "extinguished and obliterated. Here, "extinguished" (*wang*) means non-existence, and "obliterated" (*min*) means cessation.
What is the point of merely discussing these literal definitions? I ask those who hold this scroll to investigate and examine the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiaozhi*).
Generally speaking, when we say "non-existent," in what dharma does it not exist? When we speak of "extinction," is it the extinction of annihilation?
It is rather the extinction of *śānti* (quiescence). It is the quiescence of the two extremes and biased views, through which one perceives the Middle Way.

How could one claim that emptiness is attained only after the three thousand dharmas have been extinguished until not a single thing remains? Once the three thousand dharmas within a single thought-moment are free from all views, they function spontaneously.
The three truths are the unity of principle and phenomena; how could one harbor a biased interpretation that principle exists apart from phenomena?

Although Zhiyi’s "Contemplation of the Mind" has already clarified this, it must accord with the Patriarchal Texts: the three thousand realms are identical to emptiness, the three thousand realms are identical to the provisional, and the three thousand realms are identical to the Middle Way.
Furthermore, these three thousand realms are simultaneously eternal, both essence and function, and in every dharma of cultivation and nature, essence and function, there are the three truths.

That these thousand [verses] thus perfectly explain all phenomena with such wondrous subtlety—for this reason, Siming [Zhiyi] removed ignorance and revealed the distinctions of existence, manifesting the six stages of identity;

the dung beetle and the snake demonstrated the four lands; and within the gold and jewels, he revived the Tiantai tradition—a masterpiece that has remained unsurpassed through antiquity and the present.
The *Shu* says: "I am not yet fully clear on how the Three Thousand Worlds are the established dharma, and how that established dharma serves as the foundation of non-abiding.
Master Xuan’s refutation of ignorance contains a distinction between 'possessing' [the dharma] and 'being identical to' it;
this is because he does not state that the differentiated dharmas are themselves the one true reality. How true these words are!
Bian said: To examine the origin of the Four Teachings’ establishment of the basis of non-abiding through the three thousand dharmas:
it is because the basis of non-abiding is fully endowed with the established dharmas, and the established dharmas are themselves the basis of non-abiding.
Have you not heard that it is precisely because the principle is fully present that phenomenal function exists; therefore, every instance of phenomenal function is identical to the principle.
To speak of "immediacy" (*ji*) means that the whole body is such that it cannot be divided into two; these dharmas are explained as being conjoined.
This meaning has already been clearly pointed out according to the texts in the *Zhijyao* (Essentials), so there is no need for further prolix citation.

However, Master Yue takes up what Master Xuan refuted regarding Siming—that while there is only the sense of "endowment" (*ju*), there is no sense of "immediacy" (*ji*). Alas! Master Yue ascended to the level of Siming, yet...

Regarding these two gates, one may not realize that they are inherently identical and cannot be approached through separate paths. One should know that when one dharma is contrasted with all dharmas, it reveals the fundamental essence and virtues;
thus, "inclusion" (*ju*) is discussed. When two dharmas are contrasted with each other, they reveal that their fundamental wondrous essence is the same; thus, "identity" (*ji*) is discussed.
Once the distinctions arising from ignorance are removed, the meanings of both identity and inclusion are fully realized. This is the Perfect [Teaching].
The teaching that all phenomena are differentiated means that, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the provisional (*upāya*) is opened;

this provisional, by its very spontaneity, is identical in essence with the real, and is thus wondrous. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "One merely removes the illness, but does not remove the dharma.
How could one not believe this?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The wondrous bliss is like a bright mirror; the ten realms arise as images.

One should know that this contains two layers of meaning regarding the establishment of dharmas based on the non-abiding foundation (*anālaya-mūla*). First, it distinguishes the nature itself using the metaphor of the mirror to represent the true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is the non-abiding foundation;

the brightness represents the ten realms, which are the dharmas established upon that foundation. Second, it distinguishes between cultivation and nature, wherein the mirror's brightness represents both.

Taken together, these form the image of the "root of non-abiding," from which the ten realms arise; since these are the dharmas established [by that root], the dharmas of the ten realms—whether in their cultivated (prabhāvitā) or inherent (prakṛti) states—are all derivative matters.

Now, there are those who follow the *Zhijiao yaocao* and claim that the three thousand [dharmas] are all the true aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), and that this aspect is perfectly manifest such that both the cultivated and the inherent, as well as both the fundamental and the derivative, possess aspects. Yet they still say the mirror analogy has not been personally realized; how can this be so delusional?

Xiangbian said: "Now, it is said that pointing entirely to the true reality (dharmatā) as the brightness of the mirror does not preclude saying that the brightness of the mirror is fundamentally devoid of the ten realms;
yet, because there are images to be reflected, the ten realms exist. Thus, the nature is fundamentally without marks, for it is identical with cultivation."
Although it is said that the nature has characteristics and that the nature is non-existent, this non-existence is not like the absence of grit;

because it is identical with cultivation, its characteristics are perfectly manifest. This is why Siming [Zhiyuan] maintained that both the fundamental and the derivative possess characteristics, for cultivation and nature are a single essence, and essence and characteristics are identical.
Why is the analogy of taking a mirror to illustrate this dharma one of total parity? It is because both cultivation and nature equally possess characteristics.
Since it is taught that the essence and its attributes are identical and mutually inclusive, one should understand that the mirror metaphor must be taken as representing simultaneity:

clarity and the image are simultaneous, and cultivation and nature are a single essence. Although the image is not the clarity itself, it does not appear apart from it; although the clarity is not the image itself, it is not without the image.

This belongs to the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiaozhi*), which does not adopt the perspective of sequential time. If one were to adopt the perspective of sequential time, it would not be what is employed here.
However, this analogy is not something Master Yue alone failed to understand; even among those under the lineage of Siming, it is frequently said to be difficult to comprehend. A text states:
"One must understand that while self-cultivation exists solely within the void, the transformation of others involves the three thousand [realms] responding to sentient beings. Zhiyi said:

"Within the primary truth (paramārtha-satya), not a single dharma can be obtained, let alone the three thousand dharmas; yet within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), a single mind already possesses them all."
"If one can measure the Dharma in this way, how much more so the three thousand [worlds]? Jingxi said: "The three thousand worlds are all called the 'shared path';
only when they do not depart from emptiness and the middle way are they called the Buddha-way. Such explicit and clear texts are excellent for careful study and deliberation.
Bian remarked: "The masters of the Four Mountains each rely on several passages, leaving later students undecided as they take what suits their own inclinations.

More than a hundred years have passed, yet the matter still requires such laborious discernment. The masters of the mountains adhere strictly to the two aforementioned texts, yet they fail to fully perceive the obscurities within their own minds regarding the One Vehicle scriptures.
When it is said that something 'cannot be obtained,' what kind of statement is this that they study?"
One should know that this is intended to dispel attachment to words; how could it be the same as the "extinction of ash" view that destroys form and enters into emptiness?
Jingxi [Zhanran] stated that the "Three Thousand" are not the Path because they are the phenomena of the nine realms and the three modes of existence (*trivartman*);

rather, he pointed out that these very phenomena are the Buddha-realm and the three virtues (*triguṇa*), each mutually inclusive and mutually fused to constitute the Three Thousand Dharmas. Thus, the Three Thousand Worlds are all termed "not the Path," yet they are precisely what is pointed out.

If they are identical, one does not know where Master Yue intends to place the three thousand; for how could there be a "three thousand" that exists independently outside of emptiness, only to await its identification with emptiness?
In all such texts, the statement that the three thousand are "identical to emptiness and identical to the middle" points to the mutual identity of phenomena and principle.
As for the statement that the three thousand are "identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle," it refers to [the identity of] phenomena and principle.
The point regarding the contemplation of the object and the subject as a single identical essence is that they are mutually immanent. To examine Master Yue’s insight in detail:

he analyzes the perfect three truths by correlating them respectively with existence and non-existence; this is easy for beginners to understand at first glance and is convenient for the study of the Four Ming school. Some may praise it as correct, while others may slander it as erroneous.

Even if one were to strictly adhere to these two aforementioned texts, [they would still state] that the three thousand [realms] are identical to emptiness, and the three thousand [realms] are identical to [form].

How can one directly interpret the texts stating that the three thousand [realms] of the provisional are identical to the middle, and that the three thousand of both [the provisional and the middle] are simultaneously constant, simultaneous in essence, and simultaneous in function?
I have labored over the "One-Mind Three-Thousand" (Ichinen Sanzen) of the Sannō school with great effort for over twenty years.
Recently, while living in seclusion, I read the letter from Master Gō (Eshun) to Kōchi (Kōchi), as well as Kōchi’s reply to him, which was prolix...
Furthermore, I have provided only a brief and general exposition of the essential principles.

Should Master Yue encounter any further textual or doctrinal points, if they accord with these essential principles, there will be no need for further labor; may those who share my aim examine this in detail.

A General Discourse on the Five Chapters of the *Lanpen* (Ullambana): First, the Correct Meaning of the Sectarian Teachings on the Rituals for Receiving Precepts in Both Concentrated and Dispersed States;
Second, Distinguishing and Borrowing Specific Names to Apply Them Universally.

Regarding the difficulty of the *bujiao* (teachings of the specific divisions) as perceived by scholars of the Shanjia school, there are two points: first, that the *bujiao* are either "with" or "without" [the provisional];

second, that the *bujiao* are either "opened" or "not opened. As for the former point, since the period prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* had not yet opened the provisional (*kaiquan*), [the teachings were considered difficult].

Why should one consistently maintain [the distinction] that the primary teaching of the *Sixteen Contemplations* speaks only of the One Perfect [Vehicle], whereas the *Immeasurable Meanings*, being identical to the *Tattva-ghṛta* (the "cream of butter"), does not maintain this?
Why is what is taught here still said to encompass both the partial and the small vehicles? Based on this, the masters of old established four propositions to categorize them:
first, those where the section maintains the teaching but the teaching itself does not maintain it, such as the *Sixteen Contemplations*.

First, those that teach the vehicle but do not manifest the division [of the teachings], such as the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*; second, those that manifest the division but do not teach the vehicle;

third, those that manifest both the division and the teaching, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vaipulya*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras; and fourth, those that manifest neither the division nor the teaching, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*’s revelation of the provisional.
Traditionally, this has been passed down as a common saying, and it was taken as the definitive statement on the rules of our own school’s patriarchs to refute other sects.
Upon hearing this, how could one not voice the lament that the family now faces an unavoidable predicament?

Observe how Master Tiantai was able to skillfully analyze and interpret the various scriptures, such that he could walk alone at the pinnacle of the ages; this was because he profoundly grasped the intent of transformation and possessed the eye of the entire body of teachings.
Although the Dharma of the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time is like a pearl rolling upon a tray, [it is he who discerns its movement].
Nothing lies outside of this. I have examined and deliberated upon the *bùjiào* (divisional teachings), and there are certainly no four propositions [regarding their existence].

This was merely established erroneously by those of former times and has been handed down to the present; scholars must not fail to discern this. One must know that the *bùjiào* of the past were such that the "four seasons" could not be spoken of.

Whenever it is said that there are divisions and teachings, this refers to the meaning of opening up provisional means (*kāuán*) for the sake of transformation; its ultimate intent returns to the *Fahua* (Lotus Sūtra). When contrasted with the past, the present is thus revealed.

Regarding the question of whether the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*—both the Perfect (*yuan*) and the Partial (*pian*)—are "accompanied" (*dai*) or "unaccompanied": before the *Lotus*, while the Perfect was not yet revealed, both were accompanied.

Once the *Lotus* arrived and the Perfect was revealed, all [partial teachings] became unaccompanied. Now, I ask: within the main body of the Sixteen Contemplations, is the one Perfect teaching revealed or unrevealed?
If it is unrevealed, how can it be said that this teaching is "unaccompanied" by the intent of the Vaipulya transformation, given that the Perfect is used as its counterpart?
These two meanings apply universally: first, the meaning of refutation and censure; second, the meaning of accommodation and reconciliation.

How can one fail to distinguish between the different intentions behind the various categories of teachings and the variations in what is taught according to circumstances within the various scriptural collections?

One must realize that there are indeed distinct intentions behind specific categories of teachings, just as there are distinct variations in what is taught according to circumstances within specific scriptural collections—just as in the case of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Pu-fang-deng) section.
Within these [teachings], there may be cases where it is solely the Perfect (yuan), or where it encompasses the distinct (bie); they may belong to the Mahāyāna gate or pertain to all four teachings;

they may involve refutation and rejection, or lack such refutation. Judging by the purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s transformation, since the partial has not yet been opened, all are accompanied by the Perfect.
When the Perfect is contrasted with the partial, there is refutation and accommodation; when meeting the *Avataṃsaka*, it is combined with the One; and at the Deer Park, it is bestowed.
The three types of *prajñā* encompass the two [vehicles] without the need for prolix explanation.

If the *Anantārthika-sūtra* were still common to both the partial (Hīnayāna) and the Great Vehicle, it would serve as a preface to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, because that which is produced therein cannot yet produce [the ultimate fruit].

If one wishes to judge its status, it must be categorized according to the definitive teaching as belonging to the *amṛta* (nectar) flavor. It is precisely for this reason that one knows this sūtra absolutely cannot be treated as being identical to other sūtras.

To claim that all the great sutras spoken by the Elder [Mahākāśyapa]—when categorized by their respective sections—are entirely subsumed under the provisional method of "how to enter the sentence" (*juju-fa*), is laughable;
this is especially so when it exceeds even what was taught at the Deer Park. Since there are omissions, the sequence of the method of sentences is not established.

Furthermore, regarding the teachings of the various sections, some are open while others are not. One often sees those with a beginner's mind ask: "If the Perfect [Teaching] was identical in the past, why is it not so now?"

If one asks: "If the Perfect [Teaching] has reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, why is it not opened? Or, if it is opened, why is it not so in ordinary circumstances? He replies: "In terms of the teaching (*yàojiào*), it is not opened;
in terms of the section (*bù*), it must be opened. The interlocutor further interrogates: "Since it is already the One Perfect [Teaching], why must it be opened according to the section? He replies:

"Although the Perfect Teaching is the same, when contrasted with the past, the former Perfect was not yet opened because it was partial (*piān*). Therefore, speaking from the perspective of its past limitations, it must be opened."
That person further pressed me, asking, "Ultimately, what is the characteristic of opening the provisional to reveal the perfect? I replied some time ago:

"Because it can open the partial and open that which the partial cannot open. Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the single act of opening the provisional (*kaquan*) and the two purposes of the teaching (*jiaoyi*) are attained simultaneously.

Even this answer was not yet sufficient; it was only when one understands the characteristic of opening the provisional according to the teachings (*yuejiao kaquan*) that [the full meaning is realized].

This doubt will naturally be resolved; one must know that there is only the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*) according to the *nikāyas*, and no disclosure of the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) according to the *nikāyas*.

Furthermore, many students harbor doubts regarding the *Fahua wenju ji* (Commentary on the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), which states: "The perfect reality is not different [from the provisional], yet it has simply not been disclosed.

Those of the perfect vehicle at their initial stage of mind are said to be separated from the biased by the perfect; they must hear the disclosure of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. If one has already entered the reality, then one discusses only..."

Regarding this passage on "progression," why does it address only the initial stage (*ādikarmika*) and not the subsequent stages? Is this the meaning of the *śāstra* (treatise) itself, or is it the meaning of the teaching (*dharma*)?

The commentator says: "This is the meaning of the *śāstra*; there are instances where it is discussed generally according to the Dharma, and there are instances where it is distinguished specifically according to persons.

This particular text is a specific distinction made according to persons. While this explanation is correct, one must still have a deep understanding of the relationship between the *śāstra* and the teaching.

"Knowing that the first [turning] opened the provisional (kai-gen), there are both those with teachings and those who are the objects addressed by them; these objects range from the partial (hen) to the complete (en).

Regarding this passage, Jingxi [Zhiyi] simplified the initial and final stages based on the complete (en) capacity for which the teaching was intended. However, if we discuss it generally according to the opening of the provisional by means of the various vehicles (bu), as the preceding text states:
"The reality of the Complete (en-jitsu) is not different, but it has merely not been opened and manifested. These two phrases should be carefully contemplated by me.

In the *Tiantai Shibu Guan Jing Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning of the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra), prior to the clear exposition of the three contemplations for rebirth in the Pure Land and following the harmonious interpretation of the sutras and śāstras, the commentary on the scripture states:

Question: In the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma cannot attain rebirth there; yet in this sutra, it is said that even those with such heinous offenses can attain rebirth.

There are two interpretations regarding the way people commit these sins, categorized as superior and inferior. As for those of superior faculties, King Ajātaśatru is an example of one who committed a heinous crime.
There must necessarily be heavy remorse that causes one's offenses to be diminished and thinned, allowing them to attain birth as a human being;

because those who commit acts of rebellion against the Buddha generally lack such heavy remorse, they cannot attain birth. Second, regarding practice, there are the fixed and the dispersed: the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha is called "fixed," while all other virtuous karmas are described as "dispersed.
Because the power of dispersed virtues is subtle, they cannot eliminate the five rebellious acts (ānantarya-karma), nor can they enable one to proceed [to the Pure Land].

Since the fundamental basis of birth is established herein, it is said that there is no birth; yet this sutra clarifies contemplation, and thus speaks of attaining birth. Now, first, we shall explain the initial meaning.

Furthermore, remorse has degrees of lightness and heaviness depending on whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull. These faculties being sharp or dull results from differences in past habitual tendencies.

If a person of inferior faculties encounters conditions and commits a transgression against their parents, and lacks profound remorse, the sin of the transgression will not be extinguished—not only...

Those who obstruct rebirth in the Pure Land will inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell. However, if a person of superior faculties encounters conditions to commit a grave offense such as a heinous crime (ānantarya-karma), provided they feel profound remorse, the sin of the offense will certainly be extinguished.
Not only will this not obstruct rebirth in the Pure Land, but they may even enter the stages [of the bodhisattva path] and attain rootless faith (*amūla-śraddhā*), as in the case of Ajātaśatru.
While such individuals may have their sins extinguished through profound remorse, it is not necessarily the case that they will invariably attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

One must certainly generate the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land; if one lacks the power of that vow, even if one’s offenses are extinguished and one enters the stages [of the bodhisattva path], one will not necessarily attain birth there.
Although the commentary here cites only the case of King Bimbisāra’s profound repentance, in reality, King Bimbisāra had not yet generated the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Generally speaking, when discussing the extinction of offenses, there must be the efficacy of that which can extinguish them; this refers to the principle of the person, and one must point to the benefit [of the vow].
This is the power of a single moment of intense repentance by one of courageous faculties, which can immediately extinguish [the offense]; how much more so for the person who committed it.

Since there are indeed degrees of lightness and heaviness among the offenses of immediate retribution (ānantarya) committed—whether superior or inferior—it is clear that what is light is easy to extinguish while what is heavy is difficult to extinguish.
Regardless of whether the offense is light or heavy, if it has not been extinguished, those who desire rebirth will certainly be obstructed by it, even though the power of that Buddha’s vow is great.

It is indeed appropriate to exclude them. Now, regarding those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the Dharma as described in the *Sixteen Contemplations*, if their sins have not yet been extinguished, they should fall into the evil realms to undergo endless suffering;

this situation is identical to that in the *Mūla-sūtra*, where it is stated that such persons cannot attain rebirth there. How could the *Sixteen Contemplations* possibly allow one who possesses the grave offenses of the five rebellious acts to attain rebirth?
That Buddha made his vow to exclude those who commit these rebellious acts because his heart desired for all sentient beings [to be saved].
